### Energy Performance  
Samsung Electronics reported total energy consumption at business sites of 38,772 GWh in 2024 (DX Division: 4,180 GWh; DS Division: 34,592 GWh) [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_166]. Electricity accounted for 32,084 GWh, while other energy sources—including steam, LNG, LPG, petrol, and diesel—totalled 6,688 GWh [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_157][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_166]. Renewable energy consumption reached 10,069 GWh in 2024, representing a renewable energy transition rate of 31.4% globally [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_157]. By division, the DX Division achieved a 93.4% transition rate (2,884 GWh), while the DS Division reached 24.8% (7,184 GWh) [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_166]. Regionally, Samsung confirmed 100% renewable electricity usage across manufacturing sites in Korea, Vietnam, China, Brazil, and Mexico since 2022, primarily via Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs) and Renewable Energy Certificates (RECs) [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_24]. Energy intensity stood at 13.5 MWh per KRW 100 million in 2024, down from 15.4 in 2023 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_157].

### Water Management  
Total water intake was 188,540,000 tonnes in 2024, comprising 187,639,000 tonnes of municipal (surface) water and 902,000 tonnes of groundwater [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_157]. Wastewater discharge totalled 152,109,000 tonnes, while water reuse amounted to 125,463,000 tonnes—including 74,784,000 tonnes of ultra-pure water supply and 23,025,000 tonnes of recovery [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_157][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_158]. At Korean manufacturing sites (Giheung, Hwaseong, Pyeongtaek, Cheonan, Onyang), water reuse reached 101,106,000 tonnes in 2024 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_65]. All Korean sites attained Alliance for Water Stewardship (AWS) Platinum certification in 2024 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_42]. Suppliers’ water consumption was reported as 88,467,000 tonnes in 2024 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_158].

### Emissions Management  
Market-based Scope 1 and 2 GHG emissions totalled 14,546,000 tonnes CO₂e in 2024 (Scope 1: 342,000 tonnes CO₂e; Scope 2: 10,058,000 tonnes CO₂e) [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_162]. This includes newly disclosed NF₃ emissions of 1,245,000 tonnes CO₂e—the first-time reporting under updated methodology incorporating refrigerants, wastewater, and leakage [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_162][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_152]. Scope 3 emissions totalled 105,612,000 tonnes CO₂e in 2024, with “Use of sold products” constituting the largest category (82,714,000 tonnes CO₂e) [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_154]. The DS Division contributed 22,900,000 tonnes CO₂e of Scope 3 emissions in 2024, while the DX Division contributed 82,713,000 tonnes CO₂e [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_162]. Air pollutant emissions included NOₓ (729 tonnes), SOₓ (35 tonnes), and PM (90 tonnes) in 2024 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_158].

### Waste Management  
Total waste generated across divisions was 1,348,979 tonnes in 2024 (DX: 322,144 tonnes; DS: 1,026,835 tonnes), comprising general waste (910,510 tonnes), hazardous waste (12,129 tonnes), and other categories [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_166]. In Korea, the recycling rate reached 99.0% in 2024, with a target of 99.9% by 2025 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_41]. Globally, 22 manufacturing sites pursued Platinum Zero Waste-to-Landfill validation, with 12 already certified (including Gumi in Korea and sites in Hungary, Vietnam, and Malaysia) [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_31]. E-waste collection totalled 6.91 million tonnes cumulatively from 2009 to end-2024, with targets of 10 million tonnes by 2030 and 25 million tonnes by 2050 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_29][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_30].

### TCFD Strategy, Risk Management, Metrics & Targets  
Samsung Electronics integrates climate risk into its enterprise-wide Business Continuity Management System and applies a four-step process (recognition → assessment → treatment → progress management) for resource circularity and climate risks [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_29][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_42]. Physical risks (e.g., drought, flood) and transition risks (e.g., carbon pricing, regulatory shifts) are assessed using IPCC, IEA, and NGFS scenarios [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_22][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_46]. Key metrics include Scope 1+2 emissions (target: net zero by 2030 for DX Division; 2050 for DS Division), renewable energy transition rate (target: 100% for all manufacturing sites by 2025), and water reuse (target: 109 million tonnes at Korean sites by 2030) [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_22][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_42].

GRI 306 Waste: Waste diversion rate by waste stream (hazardous/non-hazardous); landfill disposal volume; waste-to-energy conversion data.

Samsung Electronics reported a Lost-Time Injury Rate (LTIR) of 0.022% in 2024, down from 0.023% in 2023 and 0.033% in 2022, based on workplace accidents resulting in one or more days of absence (excluding daily life incidents) [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_146]. The supplier LTIR was 0.035% in 2024, a decrease from 0.064% in 2023 and 0.046% in 2022, measured for Korean suppliers stationed at Samsung sites [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_146]. No major incidents were recorded in 2022–2024 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_146]. The company’s occupational health and safety management system covers all employees globally, with dedicated governance through the Global EHS Office, which establishes standards and supports implementation across workplaces and supply chains [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_76]. In 2024, approximately 3,000 risk assessment experts were trained to strengthen hazard identification and mitigation capabilities [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_98].

### Training  
In 2024, Samsung Electronics delivered an average of 66.8 training hours per employee globally, up from 58.2 hours in 2023 and 52.1 hours in 2022 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_147]. In Korea, the average was 61.2 hours per employee, compared to 77.5 hours in 2023 and 70.5 hours in 2022 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_147]. Women received slightly more training than men in 2024 (69.0 vs. 61.6 hours), while regular employees averaged 64.5 hours versus 42.3 hours for non-regular employees (subcontractors and apprentices) [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_147]. Total training expenses amounted to KRW 240.4 billion in 2024, representing 0.08% of sales and 0.6% of personnel expenses [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_147]. The company also supported re-employment for 8,001 individuals through its Career Consulting Center in 2024, achieving an 86.0% re-employment rate [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_147].

### Diversity  
The global share of female employees was 25.8% in Korea, 43.1% in Asia (Southeast Asia, Southwest Asia, China, Japan), 33.6% in North America and Latin America, 33.3% in Europe, 36.0% in CIS, and 18.9% in Middle East and Africa in 2024 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_145]. At the executive level, women constituted 7.4% of the workforce globally in 2024, up from 7.3% in 2023 and 6.9% in 2022 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_145]. Employees with disabilities numbered 1,999 in Korea in 2024, representing 1.9% of the Korean workforce [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_145]. In December 2024, Samsung Electronics joined the Valuable 500, a global initiative advancing disability inclusion [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_92].

### Supplier Social Assessment  
In 2024, 92% of Samsung’s global suppliers were comprehensively evaluated, with 75% rated “outstanding” [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_148]. Among first-tier suppliers, 59% held health and safety management system certifications (e.g., ISO 45001) in 2024, up from 51% in 2023 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_148]. Third-party audit compliance rates for social criteria included 93% for working hours, 92% for non-discrimination, 99% for prohibition of child labor, and 98% for freedom of association among first-tier suppliers in 2024 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_150]. Forced labor special audits covered 53 suppliers across five countries in 2024, and USD 14,838 in recruitment fees was returned to 41 migrant workers [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_114].

### Board Composition and Oversight Structure  
As of the end of March 2025, Samsung Electronics’ Board of Directors comprises 3 internal directors and 6 independent directors, with the roles of Board Chair and CEO formally separated to strengthen independence and transparency; independent director Je-Yoon Shin serves as Chair [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_5]. The Board functions as the company’s highest decision-making body and oversees sustainable management activities across environment, society, and governance (ESG) domains [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_5]. To institutionalize this oversight, the Governance Committee was reorganized into the Sustainability Committee under the Board in July 2021; all six independent directors participate in this committee, which deliberates and approves ESG-related management policies, mid- to long-term strategies, and risk management frameworks—including those concerning shareholder return policies [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_5]. The Board also exercises direct oversight of climate-related risks and opportunities, particularly through the Sustainability Committee, which reviewed and resolved the “New Environmental Strategy” in September 2022—encompassing long-term climate response and resource circularity goals—and has incorporated key achievements into its agenda annually since 2023 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_177][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_11][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_40].

### Anti-Corruption Governance and Compliance Systems  
Samsung Electronics maintains a zero-tolerance policy toward corruption and bribery, grounded in its Global Anti-Corruption and Bribery Policy [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_133]. All operations are assessed for corruption-related risks, and anti-corruption policies and procedures are communicated and trained across the organization [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_173]. In 2024, 138,414 individuals completed compliance training, and 254,033 individuals participated in fraud prevention training—including mandatory instruction on Korea’s Improper Solicitation and Graft Act for administrative contract employees [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_137]. The corporate Compliance Team, led by the Chief Compliance Officer, attends all Board and Management Committee meetings to support transparent decision-making and reports major issues directly to the Board [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_133]. Additionally, the externally governed Samsung Compliance Committee—established in February 2020 and comprising independent members—provides recommendations to strengthen compliance monitoring and control functions across seven major Samsung Group member companies, including Samsung Electronics [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_133]. Whistleblowing mechanisms are operationalized via dedicated channels: 1,238 compliance-related and 930 ethics-related cases were reported in 2024 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_137].

### Integration of Climate Risk into Enterprise Risk Management  
Climate-related risks and opportunities are systematically integrated into Samsung Electronics’ enterprise risk management system [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_181]. The company employs a structured Climate-Related Risk and Opportunity Analysis Process—including scenario analysis aligned with IPCC, IEA, and NGFS frameworks—to identify, assess financial impacts of, and refine responses to physical risks (e.g., floods, droughts, wildfires) and transition risks (e.g., rising carbon credit costs, shifting energy prices) across short-, medium-, and long-term horizons [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_18][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_43][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_44]. Identified risks are monitored through divisional governance bodies: the DX Division’s Environmental Safety Meetings and the DS Division’s Carbon Reduction Committee oversee GHG emission reduction tasks, while the ESG Disclosure Task Force establishes calculation standards and builds systems to meet evolving disclosure requirements [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_177][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_181]. Key risk factors are escalated to the Sustainability Committee and ESG Management Council for deliberation, response planning, and ongoing monitoring [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_181][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_44].

### Board Composition and Oversight Structure  
As of the end of March 2025, Samsung Electronics’ Board of Directors comprises 3 internal directors and 6 independent directors, with the roles of Board Chair and CEO formally separated to strengthen independence and transparency; independent director Je-Yoon Shin serves as Chair [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_5]. The Board functions as the company’s highest decision-making body and oversees sustainable management activities across environment, society, and governance (ESG) domains [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_5]. To institutionalize this oversight, the Governance Committee was reorganized into the Sustainability Committee under the Board in July 2021; all six independent directors participate in this committee, which deliberates and approves ESG-related management policies, mid- to long-term strategies, and risk management frameworks—including those concerning shareholder return policies [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_5]. The Board also exercises direct oversight of climate-related risks and opportunities, particularly through the Sustainability Committee, which reviewed and resolved the “New Environmental Strategy” in September 2022—encompassing long-term climate response and resource circularity goals—and has incorporated key achievements into its agenda annually since 2023 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_177][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_11][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_40].

### Anti-Corruption Governance and Compliance Systems  
Samsung Electronics maintains a zero-tolerance policy toward corruption and bribery, grounded in its Global Anti-Corruption and Bribery Policy [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_133]. All operations are assessed for corruption-related risks, and anti-corruption policies and procedures are communicated and trained across the organization [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_173]. In 2024, 138,414 individuals completed compliance training, and 254,033 individuals participated in fraud prevention training—including mandatory instruction on Korea’s Improper Solicitation and Graft Act for administrative contract employees [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_137]. The corporate Compliance Team, led by the Chief Compliance Officer, attends all Board and Management Committee meetings to support transparent decision-making and reports major issues directly to the Board [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_133]. Additionally, the externally governed Samsung Compliance Committee—established in February 2020 and comprising independent members—provides recommendations to strengthen compliance monitoring and control functions across seven major Samsung Group member companies, including Samsung Electronics [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_133]. Whistleblowing mechanisms are operationalized via dedicated channels: 1,238 compliance-related and 930 ethics-related cases were reported in 2024 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_137].

### Integration of Climate Risk into Enterprise Risk Management  
Climate-related risks and opportunities are systematically integrated into Samsung Electronics’ enterprise risk management system [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_181]. The company employs a structured Climate-Related Risk and Opportunity Analysis Process—including scenario analysis aligned with IPCC, IEA, and NGFS frameworks—to identify, assess financial impacts of, and refine responses to physical risks (e.g., floods, droughts, wildfires) and transition risks (e.g., rising carbon credit costs, shifting energy prices) across short-, medium-, and long-term horizons [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_18][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_43][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_44]. Identified risks are monitored through divisional governance bodies: the DX Division’s Environmental Safety Meetings and the DS Division’s Carbon Reduction Committee oversee GHG emission reduction tasks, while the ESG Disclosure Task Force establishes calculation standards and builds systems to meet evolving disclosure requirements [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_177][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_181]. Key risk factors are escalated to the Sustainability Committee and ESG Management Council for deliberation, response planning, and ongoing monitoring [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_181][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_44].

### Not covered in source material  
GRI 2-17 (Collective knowledge of the highest governance body), GRI 2-18 (Evaluation of the performance of the highest governance body), GRI 2-19 to 2-21 (Remuneration policies, determination process, and compensation ratios), GRI 205-3 (Confirmed incidents of corruption and actions taken), TCFD Metrics and Targets sub-disclosures on Scope 3 emissions metrics or absolute targets beyond 2024 progress figures, and verification details for Scope 1 and 2 emissions (e.g., assurance provider, scope of assurance) are not addressed in the provided context.

### Energy Performance  
Samsung Electronics reported total energy consumption at business sites of 38,772 GWh in 2024 (DX Division: 4,180 GWh; DS Division: 34,592 GWh) [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_166]. Electricity accounted for 32,084 GWh; other sources—including steam, LNG, LPG, petrol, and diesel—totalled 6,688 GWh [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_157][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_166]. Renewable energy consumption reached 10,069 GWh in 2024, representing a global renewable energy transition rate of 31.4% [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_157]. By division, the DX Division achieved 93.4% (2,884 GWh); the DS Division, 24.8% (7,184 GWh) [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_166]. Regionally, Samsung confirmed 100% renewable electricity usage across manufacturing sites in Korea, Vietnam, China, Brazil, and Mexico since 2022, primarily via PPAs and RECs [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_24]. Energy intensity was 13.5 MWh per KRW 100 million in 2024 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_157].

### Water Management  
Total water intake was 188,540,000 tonnes in 2024: 187,639,000 tonnes municipal (surface) water and 902,000 tonnes groundwater [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_157]. Wastewater discharge totalled 152,109,000 tonnes; water reuse amounted to 125,463,000 tonnes—including 74,784,000 tonnes of ultra-pure water supply and 23,025,000 tonnes of recovery [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_157][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_158]. At Korean manufacturing sites (Giheung, Hwaseong, Pyeongtaek, Cheonan, Onyang), water reuse reached 101,106,000 tonnes in 2024 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_65]. All Korean sites attained Alliance for Water Stewardship (AWS) Platinum certification in 2024 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_42]. Suppliers’ water consumption was 88,467,000 tonnes in 2024 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_158]. Water risk assessments using the WRI Aqueduct Water Risk Atlas identified high- or extremely high-stress regions for sites in China (Xi’an/Suzhou, Tianjin), the U.S. (Austin/Taylor), and India [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_63][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_34].

### Emissions Management  
Market-based Scope 1 and 2 GHG emissions totalled 14,546,000 tonnes CO₂e in 2024 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_162]. This comprises Scope 1 emissions of 342,000 tonnes CO₂e and Scope 2 emissions of 10,058,000 tonnes CO₂e [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_162]. NF₃ emissions were newly disclosed in 2024 at 1,245,000 tonnes CO₂e [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_162][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_152]. Scope 3 emissions totalled 105,612,000 tonnes CO₂e in 2024, with “Use of sold products” constituting 82,714,000 tonnes CO₂e—the largest category [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_154]. Air pollutant emissions included NOₓ (729 tonnes), SOₓ (35 tonnes), and PM (90 tonnes) in 2024 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_158].

### Waste Management  
Total waste generated was 1,348,979 tonnes in 2024 (DX: 322,144 tonnes; DS: 1,026,835 tonnes) [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_166]. In Korea, the recycling rate reached 99.0% in 2024, with a target of 99.9% by 2025 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_41]. Globally, 22 manufacturing sites pursued Platinum Zero Waste-to-Landfill validation; 12 were certified by end-2024, including Gumi (Korea) and sites in Hungary, Vietnam (Hồ Chí Minh), and Malaysia [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_31]. Cumulative e-waste collected from 2009 to end-2024 totalled 6.91 million tonnes, with targets of 10 million tonnes by 2030 and 25 million tonnes by 2050 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_29][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_30].

### TCFD Strategy, Risk Management, Metrics & Targets  
Samsung integrates climate risk into its Business Continuity Management System and applies a four-step process (recognition → assessment → treatment → progress management) for resource circularity and climate risks [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_29][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_42]. Physical and transition risks are assessed using IPCC, IEA, and NGFS scenarios [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_22][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_46]. Key targets include net zero Scope 1+2 emissions by 2030 (DX Division) and 2050 (DS Division), 100% renewable electricity for all manufacturing sites by 2025, and 109 million tonnes of water reuse at Korean sites by 2030 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_22][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_42].

### Energy Performance  
Samsung Electronics reported total energy consumption at business sites of 38,772 GWh in 2024 (DX Division: 4,180 GWh; DS Division: 34,592 GWh) [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_166]. Electricity accounted for 32,084 GWh, while other energy sources—including steam, LNG, LPG, petrol, and diesel—totalled 6,688 GWh [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_157][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_166]. Renewable energy consumption reached 10,069 GWh in 2024, representing a renewable energy transition rate of 31.4% globally [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_157]. By division, the DX Division achieved a 93.4% transition rate (2,884 GWh), while the DS Division reached 24.8% (7,184 GWh) [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_166]. Regionally, Samsung confirmed 100% renewable electricity usage across manufacturing sites in Korea, Vietnam, China, Brazil, and Mexico since 2022, primarily via Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs) and Renewable Energy Certificates (RECs) [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_24]. Energy intensity stood at 13.5 MWh per KRW 100 million in 2024, down from 15.4 in 2023 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_157].

### Water Management  
Total water intake was 188,540,000 tonnes in 2024, comprising 187,639,000 tonnes of municipal (surface) water and 902,000 tonnes of groundwater [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_157]. Wastewater discharge totalled 152,109,000 tonnes, while water reuse amounted to 125,463,000 tonnes—including 74,784,000 tonnes of ultra-pure water supply and 23,025,000 tonnes of recovery [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_157][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_158]. At Korean manufacturing sites (Giheung, Hwaseong, Pyeongtaek, Cheonan, Onyang), water reuse reached 101,106,000 tonnes in 2024 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_65]. All Korean sites attained Alliance for Water Stewardship (AWS) Platinum certification in 2024 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_42]. Suppliers’ water consumption was reported as 88,467,000 tonnes in 2024 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_158].

### Emissions Management  
Market-based Scope 1 and 2 GHG emissions totalled 14,546,000 tonnes CO₂e in 2024 (Scope 1: 342,000 tonnes CO₂e; Scope 2: 10,058,000 tonnes CO₂e) [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_162]. This includes newly disclosed NF₃ emissions of 1,245,000 tonnes CO₂e—the first-time reporting under updated methodology incorporating refrigerants, wastewater, and leakage [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_162][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_152]. Scope 3 emissions totalled 105,612,000 tonnes CO₂e in 2024, with “Use of sold products” constituting the largest category (82,714,000 tonnes CO₂e) [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_154]. The DS Division contributed 22,900,000 tonnes CO₂e of Scope 3 emissions in 2024, while the DX Division contributed 82,713,000 tonnes CO₂e [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_162]. Air pollutant emissions included NOₓ (729 tonnes), SOₓ (35 tonnes), and PM (90 tonnes) in 2024 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_158].

### Waste Management  
Total waste generated across divisions was 1,348,979 tonnes in 2024 (DX: 322,144 tonnes; DS: 1,026,835 tonnes), comprising general waste (910,510 tonnes), hazardous waste (12,129 tonnes), and other categories [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_166]. In Korea, the recycling rate reached 99.0% in 2024, with a target of 99.9% by 2025 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_41]. Globally, 22 manufacturing sites pursued Platinum Zero Waste-to-Landfill validation, with 12 already certified (including Gumi in Korea and sites in Hungary, Vietnam, and Malaysia) [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_31]. E-waste collection totalled 6.91 million tonnes cumulatively from 2009 to end-2024, with targets of 10 million tonnes by 2030 and 25 million tonnes by 2050 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_29][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_30].

### TCFD Strategy, Risk Management, Metrics & Targets  
Samsung Electronics integrates climate risk into its enterprise-wide Business Continuity Management System and applies a four-step process (recognition → assessment → treatment → progress management) for resource circularity and climate risks [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_29][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_42]. Physical risks (e.g., drought, flood) and transition risks (e.g., carbon pricing, regulatory shifts) are assessed using IPCC, IEA, and NGFS scenarios [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_22][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_46]. Key metrics include Scope 1+2 emissions (target: net zero by 2030 for DX Division; 2050 for DS Division), renewable energy transition rate (target: 100% for all manufacturing sites by 2025), and water reuse (target: 109 million tonnes at Korean sites by 2030) [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_22][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_42].

### Not covered in source material  
GRI 302 Energy: Location-based Scope 2 emissions breakdown by grid region; energy from on-site renewables generation (MW capacity).  
GRI 303 Water: Water stress assessments per facility; water withdrawal reduction targets versus base year (other than Korean sites); water recycling rates by site.  
GRI 305 Emissions: Scope 1 and 2 emissions disaggregated by fuel type (e.g., natural gas, coal); biogenic CO₂; black carbon.  
GRI 306 Waste: Waste diversion rate by waste stream (hazardous/non-hazardous); landfill disposal volume; waste-to-energy conversion data.  
TCFD: Detailed scenario analysis outputs (e.g., financial impact quantification per scenario); board-level oversight frequency; capital allocation toward climate resilience.

### Occupational Health and Safety  
Samsung Electronics reported a Lost-Time Injury Rate (LTIR) of 0.022% in 2024, down from 0.023% in 2023 and 0.033% in 2022, based on workplace accidents resulting in one or more days of absence (excluding daily life incidents) [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_146]. The supplier LTIR was 0.035% in 2024, a decrease from 0.064% in 2023 and 0.046% in 2022, measured for Korean suppliers stationed at Samsung sites [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_146]. No major incidents were recorded in 2022–2024 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_146]. The company’s occupational health and safety management system covers all employees globally, with dedicated governance through the Global EHS Office, which establishes standards and supports implementation across workplaces and supply chains [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_76]. In 2024, approximately 3,000 risk assessment experts were trained to strengthen hazard identification and mitigation capabilities [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_98].

### Training  
In 2024, Samsung Electronics delivered an average of 66.8 training hours per employee globally, up from 58.2 hours in 2023 and 52.1 hours in 2022 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_147]. In Korea, the average was 61.2 hours per employee, compared to 77.5 hours in 2023 and 70.5 hours in 2022 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_147]. Women received slightly more training than men in 2024 (69.0 vs. 61.6 hours), while regular employees averaged 64.5 hours versus 42.3 hours for non-regular employees (subcontractors and apprentices) [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_147]. Total training expenses amounted to KRW 240.4 billion in 2024, representing 0.08% of sales and 0.6% of personnel expenses [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_147]. The company also supported re-employment for 8,001 individuals through its Career Consulting Center in 2024, achieving an 86.0% re-employment rate [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_147].

### Diversity  
The global share of female employees was 25.8% in Korea, 43.1% in Asia (Southeast Asia, Southwest Asia, China, Japan), 33.6% in North America and Latin America, 33.3% in Europe, 36.0% in CIS, and 18.9% in Middle East and Africa in 2024 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_145]. At the executive level, women constituted 7.4% of the workforce globally in 2024, up from 7.3% in 2023 and 6.9% in 2022 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_145]. Employees with disabilities numbered 1,999 in Korea in 2024, representing 1.9% of the Korean workforce [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_145]. In December 2024, Samsung Electronics joined the Valuable 500, a global initiative advancing disability inclusion [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_92]. Per GRI 405-2, the company disclosed gender pay gaps in the UK, France, and Brazil in 2024 following wage equity surveys conducted at European sales workplaces; however, no aggregate ratio of basic salary and remuneration of women to men is provided for the global workforce [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_95]. Samsung has set a forward-looking target to increase the share of women in executive roles from 7.4% (2024 baseline) to 12% by 2030 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_95].

### Supplier Social Assessment  
In 2024, 92% of Samsung’s global suppliers were comprehensively evaluated, with 75% rated “outstanding” [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_148]. Among first-tier suppliers, 59% held health and safety management system certifications (e.g., ISO 45001) in 2024, up from 51% in 2023 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_148]. The company aims to strengthen supplier safety and health capabilities by 2030, including supporting certification attainment and post-certification consulting [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_114]. Third-party audit compliance rates for social criteria included 93% for working hours, 92% for non-discrimination, 99% for prohibition of child labor, and 98% for freedom of association among first-tier suppliers in 2024 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_150]. Forced labor special audits covered 53 suppliers across five countries in 2024, and USD 14,838 in recruitment fees was returned to 41 migrant workers [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_114].

### TCFD Strategy (social impacts of climate transition)  
Samsung Electronics’ climate transition strategy includes assessing financial impacts of transition risks—including rising energy prices and carbon credit procurement costs—as well as opportunities such as renewable energy adoption and water use reduction [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_46]. While physical risk assessments (e.g., drought, flood) incorporate site-level exposure analysis, the report does not disclose specific social dimensions of the climate transition, such as workforce reskilling needs for low-carbon manufacturing, community engagement around facility decarbonization, or just transition planning for affected workers [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_20]. The company references “enhancing our strategies against future climate change related uncertainties” and analyzing socio-economic changes under different scenarios, but no social impact assessments, stakeholder consultations, or targeted programs addressing employment, equity, or community adaptation are described [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_180].

### Not covered in source material  
No data is provided on age, ethnicity, or intersectional diversity metrics beyond gender and disability. GRI 405 requires disclosure of diversity across multiple dimensions, yet only gender and disability representation are quantified. No information is available on parental leave uptake outside Korea, inclusive hiring targets, or employee resource groups. The ratio of basic salary and remuneration of women to men is not disclosed globally—only regional pay gap analyses (UK, France, Brazil) are referenced without numerical values [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_95]. No time-bound target is stated for ISO 45001 certification among first-tier suppliers beyond the 2030 horizon for broader safety capability strengthening [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_114].

### Energy Performance  
Samsung Electronics reported total energy consumption at business sites of 38,772 GWh in 2024 (DX Division: 4,180 GWh; DS Division: 34,592 GWh) [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_166]. Electricity accounted for 32,084 GWh; other sources—including steam, LNG, LPG, petrol, and diesel—totalled 6,688 GWh [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_157][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_166]. Renewable energy consumption reached 10,069 GWh in 2024, representing a global transition rate of 31.4% [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_157]. By division, the DX Division achieved 93.4% (2,884 GWh); the DS Division, 24.8% (7,184 GWh) [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_166]. Regionally, 100% renewable electricity usage was confirmed across manufacturing sites in Korea, Vietnam, China, Brazil, and Mexico since 2022, primarily via PPAs and RECs [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_24]. Energy intensity was 13.5 MWh per KRW 100 million in 2024 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_157].

### Water Management  
Total water intake was 188,540,000 tonnes in 2024: 187,639,000 tonnes municipal (surface) water and 902,000 tonnes groundwater [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_157]. Wastewater discharge totalled 152,109,000 tonnes; water reuse amounted to 125,463,000 tonnes—including 74,784,000 tonnes ultra-pure water supply and 23,025,000 tonnes recovery [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_157][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_158]. At Korean manufacturing sites (Giheung, Hwaseong, Pyeongtaek, Cheonan, Onyang), reuse reached 101,106,000 tonnes in 2024 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_65]. All Korean sites attained AWS Platinum certification in 2024 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_42]. Samsung identified 10 facilities across India, Mexico, Poland, Egypt, China, Thailand, USA, and Indonesia as located in water-stressed regions (WRI Aqueduct Baseline Water Stress metric ≥ High(3)) [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_34][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_63]. Suppliers’ water consumption was 88,467,000 tonnes in 2024 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_158].

### Emissions Management  
Market-based Scope 1 and 2 GHG emissions totalled 14,546,000 tonnes CO₂e in 2024 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_162]. This comprises Scope 1 emissions of 342,000 tonnes CO₂e and Scope 2 emissions of 10,058,000 tonnes CO₂e; the remainder reflects newly included emissions from refrigerants, wastewater, newly designated gases, and leakage — first incorporated in 2024 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_162][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_152]. NF₃ emissions were newly disclosed at 1,245,000 tonnes CO₂e [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_162][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_152]. Scope 3 emissions totalled 105,612,000 tonnes CO₂e in 2024, with “Use of sold products” constituting 82,714,000 tonnes CO₂e — the largest category [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_154]. Air pollutants in 2024 included NOₓ (729 tonnes), SOₓ (35 tonnes), and PM (90 tonnes) [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_158].

### Waste Management  
Total waste generated was 1,348,979 tonnes in 2024 (DX: 322,144 tonnes; DS: 1,026,835 tonnes), comprising general waste (910,510 tonnes) and hazardous waste (12,129 tonnes) [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_166]. In Korea, the recycling rate was 99.0% in 2024, with a target of 99.9% by 2025 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_41]. Globally, 22 manufacturing sites pursued Platinum Zero Waste-to-Landfill validation; 12 were certified by end-2024, including Gumi (Korea) and sites in Hungary, Vietnam, and Malaysia [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_31]. Cumulative e-waste collected reached 6.91 million tonnes from 2009 to end-2024, with targets of 10 million tonnes by 2030 and 25 million tonnes by 2050 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_29][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_30].

### TCFD Strategy, Risk Management, Metrics & Targets  
Samsung integrates climate risk into its Business Continuity Management System and applies a four-step process (recognition → assessment → treatment → progress management) for resource circularity and climate risks [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_29][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_42]. Physical and transition risks are assessed using IPCC, IEA, and NGFS scenarios [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_22][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_46]. Key metrics include net zero Scope 1+2 targets (DX Division: 2030; DS Division: 2050), 100% renewable electricity for all manufacturing sites by 2025, and 109 million tonnes water reuse at Korean sites by 2030 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_22][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_42].

Samsung Electronics integrates climate risk into its enterprise-wide Business Continuity Management System and applies a four-step process (recognition → assessment → treatment → progress management) for resource circularity and climate risks [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_29][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_42]. Physical risks (e.g., drought, flood) and transition risks (e.g., carbon pricing, regulatory shifts) are assessed using IPCC, IEA, and NGFS scenarios [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_22][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_46]. Key metrics include Scope 1+2 emissions (target: net zero by 2030 for DX Division; 2050 for DS Division), renewable energy transition rate (target: 100% for all manufacturing sites by 2025), and water reuse (target: 109 million tonnes at Korean sites by 2030) [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_22][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_42].

GRI 303 Water: Water stress assessments per facility; water withdrawal reduction targets versus base year (other than Korean sites); water recycling rates by site.  
GRI 305 Emissions: Scope 1 and 2 emissions disaggregated by fuel type (e.g., natural gas, coal); biogenic CO₂; black carbon.  
GRI 306 Waste: Waste diversion rate by waste stream (hazardous/non-hazardous); landfill disposal volume; waste-to-energy conversion data.  
TCFD: Detailed scenario analysis outputs (e.g., financial impact quantification per scenario); board-level oversight frequency; capital allocation toward climate resilience.

### Occupational Health and Safety  
Samsung Electronics reported a Lost-Time Injury Rate (LTIR) of 0.022% in 2024, down from 0.023% in 2023 and 0.033% in 2022, based on workplace accidents resulting in one or more days of absence (excluding daily life incidents) [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_146]. The supplier LTIR was 0.035% in 2024, a decrease from 0.064% in 2023 and 0.046% in 2022, measured for Korean suppliers stationed at Samsung sites [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_146]. No major incidents were recorded in 2022–2024 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_146]. The company’s occupational health and safety management system covers all employees globally, with dedicated governance through the Global EHS Office, which establishes standards and supports implementation across workplaces and supply chains [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_76]. In 2024, approximately 3,000 risk assessment experts were trained to strengthen hazard identification and mitigation capabilities [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_98].

### Training  
In 2024, Samsung Electronics delivered an average of 66.8 training hours per employee globally, up from 58.2 hours in 2023 and 52.1 hours in 2022 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_147]. In Korea, the average was 61.2 hours per employee, compared to 77.5 hours in 2023 and 70.5 hours in 2022 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_147]. Women received slightly more training than men in 2024 (69.0 vs. 61.6 hours), while regular employees averaged 64.5 hours versus 42.3 hours for non-regular employees (subcontractors and apprentices) [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_147]. Total training expenses amounted to KRW 240.4 billion in 2024, representing 0.08% of sales and 0.6% of personnel expenses [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_147]. The company also supported re-employment for 8,001 individuals through its Career Consulting Center in 2024, achieving an 86.0% re-employment rate [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_147].

### Diversity  
The global share of female employees was 25.8% in Korea, 43.1% in Asia (Southeast Asia, Southwest Asia, China, Japan), 33.6% in North America and Latin America, 33.3% in Europe, 36.0% in CIS, and 18.9% in Middle East and Africa in 2024 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_145]. At the executive level, women constituted 7.4% of the workforce globally in 2024, up from 7.3% in 2023 and 6.9% in 2022 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_145]. Employees with disabilities numbered 1,999 in Korea in 2024, representing 1.9% of the Korean workforce [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_145]. In December 2024, Samsung Electronics joined the Valuable 500, a global initiative advancing disability inclusion [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_92]. Per GRI 405-2, the company disclosed gender pay gaps in the UK, France, and Brazil in 2024 following wage equity surveys conducted at European sales workplaces; however, no aggregate ratio of basic salary and remuneration of women to men is provided for the global workforce [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_95]. Samsung has set a forward-looking target to increase the share of women in executive roles from 7.4% (2024 baseline) to 12% by 2030 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_95].

### Supplier Social Assessment  
In 2024, 92% of Samsung’s global suppliers were comprehensively evaluated, with 75% rated “outstanding” [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_148]. Among first-tier suppliers, 59% held health and safety management system certifications (e.g., ISO 45001) in 2024, up from 51% in 2023 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_148]. The company aims to strengthen supplier safety and health capabilities by 2030, including supporting certification attainment and post-certification consulting [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_114]. Third-party audit compliance rates for social criteria included 93% for working hours, 92% for non-discrimination, 99% for prohibition of child labor, and 98% for freedom of association among first-tier suppliers in 2024 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_150]. Forced labor special audits covered 53 suppliers across five countries in 2024, and USD 14,838 in recruitment fees was returned to 41 migrant workers [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_114].

### TCFD Strategy (social impacts of climate transition)  
Samsung Electronics’ climate transition strategy includes assessing financial impacts of transition risks—including rising energy prices and carbon credit procurement costs—as well as opportunities such as renewable energy adoption and water use reduction [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_46]. While physical risk assessments (e.g., drought, flood) incorporate site-level exposure analysis, the report does not disclose specific social dimensions of the climate transition, such as workforce reskilling needs for low-carbon manufacturing, community engagement around facility decarbonization, or just transition planning for affected workers [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_20]. The company references “enhancing our strategies against future climate change related uncertainties” and analyzing socio-economic changes under different scenarios, but no social impact assessments, stakeholder consultations, or targeted programs addressing employment, equity, or community adaptation are described [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_180].

### Not covered in source material  
No data is provided on age, ethnicity, or intersectional diversity metrics beyond gender and disability. GRI 405 requires disclosure of diversity across multiple dimensions, yet only gender and disability representation are quantified. No information is available on parental leave uptake outside Korea, inclusive hiring targets, or employee resource groups. The ratio of basic salary and remuneration of women to men is not disclosed globally—only regional pay gap analyses (UK, France, Brazil) are referenced without numerical values [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_95]. No time-bound target is stated for ISO 45001 certification among first-tier suppliers beyond the 2030 horizon for broader safety capability strengthening [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_114].

### Board Composition and Oversight Structure  
As of the end of March 2025, Samsung Electronics’ Board of Directors comprises 3 internal directors and 6 independent directors, with the roles of Board Chair and CEO formally separated to strengthen independence and transparency; independent director Je-Yoon Shin serves as Chair [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_5]. The Board functions as the company’s highest decision-making body and oversees sustainable management activities across environment, society, and governance (ESG) domains [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_5]. To institutionalize this oversight, the Governance Committee was reorganized into the Sustainability Committee under the Board in July 2021; all six independent directors participate in this committee, which deliberates and approves ESG-related management policies, mid- to long-term strategies, and risk management frameworks—including those concerning shareholder return policies [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_5]. The Board’s collective expertise spans finance, law, IT (robotics, AI, semiconductors), risk management, public sector, and sustainable management, as documented in the Board Skills Matrix (BSM); two of the six independent directors are women, reflecting deliberate attention to gender diversity for balanced decision-making [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_5]. The Sustainability Committee reviewed and resolved the “New Environmental Strategy” in September 2022—encompassing long-term climate response and resource circularity goals—and has incorporated key achievements into its agenda annually since 2023 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_177][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_11][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_40].

### Anti-Corruption Governance and Compliance Systems  
Samsung Electronics maintains a zero-tolerance policy toward corruption and bribery, grounded in its Global Anti-Corruption and Bribery Policy [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_133]. All operations are assessed for corruption-related risks, and anti-corruption policies and procedures are communicated and trained across the organization [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_173]. In 2024, 138,414 individuals completed compliance training and 254,033 individuals participated in fraud prevention training—including mandatory instruction on Korea’s Improper Solicitation and Graft Act for administrative contract employees [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_137]. Supplier third-party audit data shows that in 2024, the “Training” compliance rate across first- and second-tier suppliers stood at 94% and 76%, respectively [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_151]. However, no time-bound target for achieving 100% ethics training coverage across first- and second-tier suppliers is disclosed in the source material. The corporate Compliance Team, led by the Chief Compliance Officer, attends all Board and Management Committee meetings to support transparent decision-making and reports major issues directly to the Board [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_133]. Additionally, the externally governed Samsung Compliance Committee—established in February 2020 and comprising independent members—provides recommendations to strengthen compliance monitoring and control functions across seven major Samsung Group member companies, including Samsung Electronics [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_133]. Whistleblowing mechanisms are operationalized via dedicated channels: 1,238 compliance-related and 930 ethics-related cases were reported in 2024 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_137]. Confirmed incidents of corruption and actions taken are not disclosed in the provided context [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_173].

### Integration of Climate Risk into Enterprise Risk Management  
Climate-related risks and opportunities are systematically integrated into Samsung Electronics’ enterprise risk management system [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_181]. The company employs a structured Climate-Related Risk and Opportunity Analysis Process—including scenario analysis aligned with IPCC, IEA, and NGFS frameworks—to identify, assess financial impacts of, and refine responses to physical risks (e.g., floods, droughts, wildfires) and transition risks (e.g., rising carbon credit costs, shifting energy prices) across short-, medium-, and long-term horizons [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_18][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_43][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_44]. Identified risks are monitored through divisional governance bodies: the DX Division’s Environmental Safety Meetings and the DS Division’s Carbon Reduction Committee oversee GHG emission reduction tasks, while the ESG Disclosure Task Force establishes calculation standards and builds systems to meet evolving disclosure requirements [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_177][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_181]. Key risk factors are escalated to the Sustainability Committee and ESG Management Council for deliberation, response planning, and ongoing monitoring [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_181][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_44]. The Board’s performance evaluation process—including methodology and results—is not disclosed in the provided context [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_171][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_172].

### Not covered in source material  
GRI 2-13 (target for gender diversity on the Board) is not disclosed: no baseline, target value, or deadline for increasing women’s representation beyond the current two out of six independent directors is stated [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_5]. GRI 2-18 (Board performance evaluation methodology and results), GRI 2-19 to 2-21 (remuneration policies, determination process, and annual total compensation ratio), and GRI 205-3 (confirmed incidents of corruption and remedial actions) are explicitly absent from the source material [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_171][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_172][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_173]. TCFD Metrics and Targets disclosures—including quantified, time-bound Scope 3 GHG targets, absolute emissions reduction goals with baselines and deadlines, or metrics tied to executive remuneration beyond general inclusion in KPIs—are not provided [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_177][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_178]. No quantified, time-bound governance or anti-corruption target (e.g., 100% supplier ethics training by 2027, whistleblower resolution timeframe, or Board gender target) is stated in the source material.

### Board Composition and Oversight Structure  
As of the end of March 2025, Samsung Electronics’ Board of Directors comprises 3 internal directors and 6 independent directors, with the roles of Board Chair and CEO formally separated to strengthen independence and transparency; independent director Je-Yoon Shin serves as Chair [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_5]. The Board functions as the company’s highest decision-making body and oversees sustainable management activities across environment, society, and governance (ESG) domains [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_5]. To institutionalize this oversight, the Governance Committee was reorganized into the Sustainability Committee under the Board in July 2021; all six independent directors participate in this committee, which deliberates and approves ESG-related management policies, mid- to long-term strategies, and risk management frameworks—including those concerning shareholder return policies [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_5]. The Board’s collective expertise spans finance, law, IT (robotics, AI, semiconductors), risk management, public sector, and sustainable management, as documented in the Board Skills Matrix (BSM); two of the six independent directors are women, reflecting deliberate attention to gender diversity for balanced decision-making [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_5]. The Sustainability Committee reviewed and resolved the “New Environmental Strategy” in September 2022—encompassing long-term climate response and resource circularity goals—and has incorporated key achievements into its agenda annually since 2023 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_177][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_11][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_40].

### Anti-Corruption Governance and Compliance Systems  
Samsung Electronics maintains a zero-tolerance policy toward corruption and bribery, grounded in its Global Anti-Corruption and Bribery Policy [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_133]. All operations are assessed for corruption-related risks, and anti-corruption policies and procedures are communicated and trained across the organization [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_173]. In 2024, 138,414 individuals completed compliance training and 254,033 individuals participated in fraud prevention training—including mandatory instruction on Korea’s Improper Solicitation and Graft Act for administrative contract employees [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_137]. However, supplier third-party audit data shows that in 2024, the “Training” compliance rate across first- and second-tier suppliers stood at 94% and 76%, respectively—indicating gaps in implementation depth beyond direct employees; remediation includes targeted capacity-building programs for high-risk tiers [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_151]. The corporate Compliance Team, led by the Chief Compliance Officer, attends all Board and Management Committee meetings to support transparent decision-making and reports major issues directly to the Board [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_133]. Additionally, the externally governed Samsung Compliance Committee—established in February 2020 and comprising independent members—provides recommendations to strengthen compliance monitoring and control functions across seven major Samsung Group member companies, including Samsung Electronics [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_133]. Whistleblowing mechanisms are operationalized via dedicated channels: 1,238 compliance-related and 930 ethics-related cases were reported in 2024 [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_137]. Confirmed incidents of corruption and actions taken are not disclosed in the provided context [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_173].

### Integration of Climate Risk into Enterprise Risk Management  
Climate-related risks and opportunities are systematically integrated into Samsung Electronics’ enterprise risk management system [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_181]. The company employs a structured Climate-Related Risk and Opportunity Analysis Process—including scenario analysis aligned with IPCC, IEA, and NGFS frameworks—to identify, assess financial impacts of, and refine responses to physical risks (e.g., floods, droughts, wildfires) and transition risks (e.g., rising carbon credit costs, shifting energy prices) across short-, medium-, and long-term horizons [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_18][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_43][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_44]. Climate scenario analysis revealed material unmitigated exposures, particularly in medium- to long-term transition risks—including insufficient alignment with customer demand for low-carbon products and rising R&D costs for low-carbon technologies—which are being addressed through expanded participation in global decarbonization initiatives and accelerated product-level life cycle assessment (LCA) rollout [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_43][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_18]. Identified risks are monitored through divisional governance bodies: the DX Division’s Environmental Safety Meetings and the DS Division’s Carbon Reduction Committee oversee GHG emission reduction tasks, while the ESG Disclosure Task Force establishes calculation standards and builds systems to meet evolving disclosure requirements [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_177][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_181]. Key risk factors are escalated to the Sustainability Committee and ESG Management Council for deliberation, response planning, and ongoing monitoring [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_181][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_44]. The Board’s performance evaluation process is not disclosed in the provided context [Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_171][Samsung_Electronics_Sustainability_Report_2025_ENG_chunk_172].
